title: Bhagwan Bazaar
meta_description: Regional Indian deities and temple motifs produced as 3D-printed tabletop objects. Wholesale and white-label line sheet.
dek: Regional deities and temple motifs, reduced to tabletop objects and produced to order on FDM machines. Every piece in the range is drawn from a specific place — a Kerala caparison, a Chola bronze, an Odia temple wheel — and modelled to hold that detail at desk scale.
dek_2: Supplied wholesale and white-label. Finishes, dimensions and colourways can be varied per order, and we manufacture to custom design — send an image of the piece you want and we model it and print it. The range below is the standing catalogue, not a limit.

notes.heading: Materials
notes.body: PLA for fine surface detail and metal-filled finishes; ABS and ASA where the piece needs heat or UV tolerance; PETG where it will be handled or hung. Material can be substituted per order.

notes.heading: Finishing
notes.body: Metal-filled prints are hand-polished on the raised surfaces so the recesses stay dark. Stone finishes are a filled-and-sealed process. Unfinished pieces ship with layer lines intact for buyers who paint in-house.

notes.heading: White-label
notes.body: Pieces can be produced without our marking, with your own base engraving, or in a colourway matched to your range. Packaging is specified per order.

notes.heading: Ordering
notes.body: Quantities, lead times and landed pricing are quoted per enquiry — volume and finish move the number considerably. Sample sets are available before a first order.

items.name: Nettipattam
items.description: The gilded crescent that fronts a temple elephant at Thrissur Pooram, worked in Kerala as rows of embossed bosses over cloth. Held here as a standing plate: concentric domes printed in brass-filled filament, polished on the crowns so they catch light the way beaten metal does.

items.name: Nataraja
items.description: Shiva in the ananda tandava, ringed by the prabhavali of flame with Apasmara underfoot. Modelled to the Chola bronze proportions rather than the modern souvenir form, and printed in bronze-filled filament that darkens in the recesses as it is handled.

items.name: Hoysala shrine
items.description: The stellate plan of Belur and Halebidu compressed to a desk-scale shrine — rotated square bases, lathe-turned pillars, a deep eave that throws the shadow line the originals depend on. Printed in ABS and stone-finished to read as the region's soft chloritic schist.

items.name: Bathukamma
items.description: Telangana stacks the Bathukamma in conical tiers of seasonal flowers around a central lamp, then floats it on water at the close of the festival. Rendered as a seven-tier form in matte PLA — the arrangement kept, the impermanence set aside.

items.name: Ganpati
items.description: The Maharashtrian domestic form for Ganesh Chaturthi, seated with modak in hand. Finished to imitate shadu — the pale river silt used for idols meant to dissolve on immersion — on a piece built to be kept and brought out each year instead.

items.name: Konark chakra
items.description: One of the twenty-four wheels of the Sun Temple chariot at Konark, each carved as a working sundial across eight major and eight minor spokes. The largest plate in the range, printed in ASA for UV stability so it holds up in a window or a lit display case.

items.name: Toran
items.description: The Gujarati threshold hanging strung above a doorway to mark an auspicious entry, traditionally beadwork, mirror and hand embroidery. Printed as a single span in matte PETG, which takes handling and humidity better than PLA where a piece is mounted and left.

items.name: Kumartuli form
items.description: Kolkata's Kumartuli quarter builds Durga up over a straw and clay armature, and the unpainted stage has a following of its own. Shipped deliberately unfinished — layer lines standing in for the potter's tool marks, surface ready for the buyer's own paint.

items.name: Ram Mandir
items.description: The Ayodhya temple in the Nagara idiom — tiered shikhara, the mandapa sequence, a carved plinth running the full footprint. The most surface area of anything in the range, and the piece that rewards the stone finish most across a wide elevation.
